## 1. Intro to openPRoT

*This section exists primarily for the benefit of readers who are new to openPRoT*

### Problem statement

Firmware runs at the bottom of the software stack, interacting directly with the hardware. A computer or server may have several microprocessors each controlling a separate device (such as a network card). How can we verify that it has not been tampered with by an attacker?

A **Platform Root of Trust (PRoT)** is a small, dedicated security chip on the motherboard that guards against this. For example, it may

- Verify the signed hash distributed with the firmware binary using its public key, and fail to boot if the authenticity of the binary cannot be verified.
- Similarly, a firmware update may fail if the authenticity of the binary cannot be verified.
- Providing attestation: a remote party can ask what firmware the chip is running and get an answer it can trust.
- Monitoring hardware. For example, watching the traffic on the flash chips that hold other devices' firmware.

`docs/src/specification/services/fwupdate.md` and `docs/src/specification/services/attestation.md` provide more detail on those two bullet points, respectively.

### Solution

**openPRoT** is a Rust-based open-source firmware stack. The aim is a shared, auditable, vendor-neutral implementation that hardware makers can adopt, rather than each vendor writing its own closed one.


| Layer | Description | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **Kernel** | `pw_kernel`, a small microkernel from Google's Pigweed project. It runs separate programs ("apps") in isolation and lets them communicate over IPC. | `third_party/pigweed` |
| **Hardware support** | Drivers for each supported chip: I2C, SPI, flash controller, GPIO, crypto accelerator, etc. | `target/`, `drivers/` |
| **Hardware abstraction (HAL)** | Common interfaces, so services above don't depend on a particular chip. | `hal/`, `platform/` |
| **Services** | Separate apps that do the security work: talking to other devices, running firmware updates, etc. | `services/` |
| **Orchestrator** | The state machine that decides when devices boot, when an update may proceed, and what to do on failure. | `services/orchestrator` |


### Targets

| Target | What it is | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ASPEED AST1060 / AST10x0** | A commercial RoT chip used on real server boards | Main development and demo platform. openPRoT examples support the AST1060 Test Harness board. Customer EVB for the AST1060 is not specifically supported at this time. There is also emulation support via QEMU. | `target/ast10x0`, `target/ast10x0/BOARDS.md`, `target/ast10x0/README.md` |
| **OpenTitan Earl Grey** | An open-source silicon root of trust | Substantial work on a separate branch. There is an example project of the Pigweed kernel running on this chip. Has CW310, CW340, Verilator and QEMU runners | `target/earlgrey/README.md` |
| **Caliptra / VeeR** | An open-source RoT core, run in an emulator or on an FPGA (the latter is tagged as manual). | Basic support | `target/veer/caliptra_emulator_main.rs`, `target/veer/workflow.json` |


### Communication protocols in openPRoT

The RoT has to communicate with the devices it protects. openPRoT uses the following industry-standard protocols:

| Protocol | Description / use case | Source |
|---|---|---|
| SPDM (Security Protocol and Data Model) | Authenticating the device and the firmware it is running (attestation, secure sessions). | `services/spdm/` |
| PLDM (Platform Level Data Model) | Firmware updates and platform monitoring. | `services/pldm/` |
| MCTP (Management Component Transport Protocol) | The message transport that carries all DMTF protocols. There is a Rust crate implementing MCTP-over-I2C. | `services/mctp/transport-i2c/README.md` |
| I2C / I3C | The bus between chips | |

The three software protocols (SPDM, PLDM, MCTP) are documented in `docs/src/specification/middleware/`. They all fall under the DMTF standards.

Most of the past year's work has been building this stack: the I2C driver, MCTP, SPDM, PLDM, and the orchestrator that uses them.

## 2. Branches in openPRoT and their status

This section summarises each remote branch, based on its git history compared with `origin/main`. There are 28 remote branches. `sync/main-to-earlgrey-hwe` is an automation branch identical to `main`, so it is omitted. The Status column uses these labels:

- **Probably in main:** most of the branch's commit messages also appear in `main`, so the work was most likely merged (typically squashed into one commit, which hides the link to the branch). This is inferred from matching commit messages, rather than by checking against merged pull requests on GitHub.
- **Not in main:** none of the branch's commit messages appear in `main`, so the work has not been merged.
- **Mostly in main:** some commits appear in `main` and some do not.


### 2.1 Current demo work (September–October 2026)

These four branches are stacked: each contains the one before it. Together they build up the OCP global demo, in which a RoT receives a firmware update over PLDM, writes it to flash, and restarts a protected device from the new image.

#### `cq-demo-integration`: 111 commits ahead (Christina Quast 63, JesseMelon 34, Anthony Rocha 13, Chris Frantz 1)

- **Purpose:** bring together the orchestrator, the flash service and the PLDM firmware update path for the OCP demo.
- **Implemented:**
  - **Flash service:** a separate app that other apps call over IPC to read, erase and write flash chips, so only one component touches the hardware. It talks to the AST10x0's flash controller. A QEMU model of the flash chip lets it be tested without hardware.
  - **Automatic flash sizing:** flash chips carry a standard table (SFDP, defined by JEDEC standard JESD216) describing their size and page layout. A new parser reads it, so the code no longer hard-codes the layout of each flash chip.
  - **Flash controller driver rework:** the driver now uses Rust's type system to enforce setup order. It cannot read or write until timing calibration has been done, and the compiler rejects code that tries.
  - **Update pump:** the loop that receives a firmware image in chunks over PLDM and writes it into a staging area in flash, ready to be checked and activated.
  - **Configuration and docs:** the config describing the platform's devices was split into smaller modules, and each component is now declared once. A new page documents which parts of the system are trusted and which are not.
  - **The RoT's own updates:** at boot, the RoT works out whether its last self-update succeeded, and either confirms or reverts it. It can also raise its anti-rollback floor.
- **Failed / fixed:** CI had been failing on every pull request since #512, because of a code-style error flagged by the Rust linter (clippy). It was fixed here.

#### `i2c-mctp-throughput`: 120 commits ahead (mostly Christina Quast and JesseMelon; Anthony Rocha 14)

- **Purpose:** the above, plus a test measuring how fast MCTP messages travel over the I2C bus.
- **Implemented:**
  - **Throughput test (Anthony Rocha):** one board sends messages and another echoes them back, to measure data rate. It is in `target/ast10x0/tests/mctp/throughput`.
  - **Update pump improvements (Christina Quast):**
    - The image is now checked in chunks as it arrives, and a failure of the checker itself is reported separately from a bad image.
    - After an update is activated, the RoT checks the whole platform again, because the device has restarted on new firmware.
    - After a new image proves itself, the spare slot is brought up to date so the fallback is not left on the old version. Only then is the anti-rollback floor raised.
- **Design decision:** the spare slot is updated by sending the image a second time, not by copying between slots, because copying needs a way to name slots that does not exist yet. The cost is a second full transfer. Devices that track their own version skip this step.

#### `ocp-global-demo`: 141 commits ahead (Christina Quast 71, JesseMelon 54, Anthony Rocha 15, Chris Frantz 1)

- **Purpose:** the Raspberry Pi-driven OCP global demo. A mock baseboard management chip (BMC) receives a firmware update through the RoT and boots it.
- **Implemented (mostly JesseMelon):**
  - **Resetting the mock BMC:** the RoT can restart the mock BMC after an update by driving a hardware pin (GPIOK5).
  - **Shared flash:** the update is written to a flash chip that both the RoT and the mock BMC can read, and the mock BMC boots from it.
  - **A real image:** the update is a working, bootable image. The mock BMC boots from the image it was just sent and reports a bumped version number to prove it.
  - **Running from the Pi:** the demo can be deployed and run from a Raspberry Pi, with a terminal dashboard (tmux) and tidied log output.
- **Anthony Rocha:** shrank the firmware update images to fit under 640 KiB.

#### `ocp-global-demo-wip`: 157 commits ahead (Christina Quast 109, JesseMelon 34, Anthony Rocha 13, Chris Frantz 1)

- **Purpose:** the integration and testing branch for the demo.
- **Implemented (mostly Christina Quast):**
  - **Full-update test:** one emulated test running the whole chain. The protected device boots under the RoT's supervision, an update arrives over PLDM, the device stages and verifies it, and the RoT activates it. The device then restarts, boots the new image and reports ready a second time. Only after that is the anti-rollback floor raised.
  - **Failure-case tests:** the update must be refused or abandoned correctly when either: the device never starts; the device fails to come back after reset; one data request fails; the sender cancels mid-transfer; or an update is offered to a RoT that is not supervising anything.
  - **Image fingerprint:** a new component computes a hash of an image while it is being verified, so it can later be reported for attestation.
  - **Test stand-ins:** a mock downstream device, plus a loopback transport that lets MCTP run without a physical bus.
  - **Crypto service protocol:** a defined message format and client library for apps to request cryptographic operations (such as verifying a flash region) from the crypto service.
  - **Docs:** a page on what the orchestrator cannot check during an update.
- **Failed / fixed:**
  - The first version of the full-update test passed even though the device never restarted. It was fixed by making the RoT, not the device, decide the final result.
  - Merging other branches broke two test builds, which were then repaired.
  - The PLDM library reports "retry timer has not elapsed" with the same error code it uses for a real fault, so a device told to wait ended its session instead. This is patched with a workaround marked temporary. The proper fix belongs in the PLDM library itself.

| `mctp-lib-main` | Evan Chuchen | Updates the external MCTP library dependency to follow its `main` branch. | Not in main |

### 2.2 Earl Grey (OpenTitan)

#### `earlgrey-hwe`: 115 commits ahead, 261 behind (Chris Frantz about 86, Anthony Chen 13, Anthony Rocha 7, Chia-Wei Liu 6, Miguel Osorio 2)

- **Purpose:** hardware enablement for the OpenTitan Earl Grey chip, led by Chris Frantz. This is the "separate branch" referred to in the Targets table.
- **Implemented:**
  - **USB:** a hardware abstraction layer and protocol stack, including USB serial (CDC-ACM) and USB firmware update (DFU 1.1).
  - **Drivers:** UART (serial), on-chip flash, SPI host, GPIO and pin configuration.
  - **Logging:** zfmt, a compact structured logging library.
  - **Update firmware:** firmware that receives updates over USB, including ownership transfer (handing control of the chip's signing keys to a new owner).
  - **Update manager:** writes firmware into the chip's own flash, scans an external SPI flash for updates, stores the owner information, and is tested across all A/B slot combinations.
  - **Services and tooling:** platform and system manager services, an updated OpenTitan toolchain bundle, and dummy signing keys for testing.
- **Failed / tried:** no abandoned work is visible in the history.
- **Note:** `sync/main-to-earlgrey-hwe` is the bot branch that merges `main` into this one. This branch is 261 commits behind `main`, so it has drifted far.

## 4. What the code does

This section describes the repository at the level of crates and modules. It describes `main` first, then the major differences that may exist on other branches. Finally, it describes features yet to be implemented on any branch.

- **main:** the shared baseline.
- **demo branches:** `ocp-global-demo-wip`, which contains `ocp-global-demo`, `i2c-mctp-throughput` and `cq-demo-integration`, with a few exceptions noted below. These are only 2 commits behind `main`.
- **`earlgrey-hwe`:** a fork from late June, 261 commits behind `main`. It has none of the orchestrator, PLDM or ast10x0 code.
- **Older branches** (`ocp-emea-demo*`, `mctp-echo-pigweed-wmarone`, `spdm-measurements`): forks from before the orchestrator existed.

This survey was done by reading file lists, READMEs, module documentation and TODO markers. Nothing was built or run, and I did not read every line of the largest files. "Complete" below is a judgement from reading the code, not from test results.

### 4.1 Repository layout

| Directory | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `services/` | The apps that do the security work: orchestrator, PLDM, SPDM, MCTP, I2C, plus flash and crypto on some branches. |
| `hal/` | The hardware abstraction layer: hardware-neutral interfaces (Rust traits) for crypto, I2C, GPIO, flash etc. |
| `platform/` | Implementations of the HAL interfaces, so services can run on different operating systems or on mocks. |
| `drivers/` | Userspace drivers. `main` has only a USART (serial) driver. |
| `target/` | Everything specific to one chip or board: `ast10x0`, `earlgrey`, `veer`. |
| `util/` | Shared helper crates: error codes, IPC wrappers, I/O traits and low-level register helpers. |
| `tools/` | Developer tools: an I2C bus monitor and an SGPIO board-config generator. |
| `docs/` | The specification and design documents. |
| `presubmit/`, `pw` | Checks run before a change is accepted (license headers, include guards, Pigweed version roll), and a wrapper script. |
| `openprot/` | A placeholder "hello world" crate. |

### 4.2 Services

#### Orchestrator (`services/orchestrator`)

The orchestrator is a state machine that decides the boot order of the platform. It verifies each protected device's firmware, releases the device from reset in order, then watches whether it boots.

| Crate | Description | Branches |
|---|---|---|
| `sm` | The state machine, with no hardware access. Events go in and requested actions come out. States run from power-on reset through supervision, waiting for devices to report ready, normal operation, updating or recovering, to locked. Each device has a failure policy: required, isolable (only that device is cut off) or cascading (devices that depend on it are also cut off). This is the most complete piece, with a large test suite. | main. On the demo branches it is split into role modules and extended to run the update flow. |
| `capabilities` | The list of things (contract only) the orchestrator can ask a device to do, as traits: control boot, hold the anti-rollback floor, read boot evidence, watch boot progress, accept updates, trial-boot a new image, recover, and latch a lockdown. | main. Demo branches add `self_update`, `device_trial_boot`, `measurer` (hash an image), `incremental_verifier` and `progress`. |
| `config` | Tables of devices per-board and their checkpoints. It is built with compile-time functions, so an invalid table fails the build. | main. Demo branches add the chain, layout (slots and golden images) and record (data kept across resets) modules. |
| `driver` | Carries out the state machine's requested actions. On `main` it reads and verifies firmware, releases and asserts reset, and commits the anti-rollback floor. Other actions (recover, authenticate, stage, activate, discard, sign attestation, lock down) deliberately fail safe with an error. | main. On the demo branches there is (`driver/update.rs`) to run the update. |
| `adapters` | Connect the orchestrator to real hardware (GPIO reset and boot-ready pins), to checkpoint walking with timeouts, and to PLDM (an accepted update request becomes an orchestrator event). | main. Demo branches add GPIO reset-control and ready-monitor adapters. |
| `timer` | Folds the boot and commit watchdog timers into one deadline. | main |
| `server` | Binds the timers to the kernel clock. It has no event loop or `main` of its own. | main |
| `test` | A mock board table and a model of one-time-programmable (OTP) memory. | main |
| `update-api` | The hand-off between an update source and the orchestrator: offer an update, write chunks (at most 512 bytes per call), complete it, then poll. | Demo branches only |

#### PLDM (`services/pldm`)

PLDM is the protocol used for firmware updates and monitoring.

| Service | Description | Branches |
|---|---|---|
| `pldm` service | The firmware device side. It wraps an external PLDM state machine library and carries PLDM messages over MCTP. It talks directly to a remote update agent. | main. `pldm-fd-run-once` adds `run_until`, so a caller can decide when to stop. |
| `api`, `client`, `server` | An IPC layer between the orchestrator and the PLDM firmware device. | Demo branches only |
| `gate` | A policy hook that decides whether an update phase may proceed. The demo branch implementation always allows the update, and the README says this must not make it onto a production device. | Demo branches only |

#### SPDM (`services/spdm`)

SPDM is the protocol for authenticating a device and reporting what firmware it runs. All the crates wrap an external SPDM library from 9elements.

- `responder`: answers SPDM requests.
- `requester`: only builds the SPDM context. Its README says protocol operations are not yet implemented.
- `transport-mctp`: carries SPDM over MCTP.
- `hash`, `rng`: give the SPDM library hashing and random numbers by calling a crypto service. On `main` the crypto client behind them is a stub that always fails.
- `common`: shared constants.

#### MCTP (`services/mctp`)

MCTP is the transport that carries the other protocols.

- `api`: the traits and wire encoding for sending and receiving messages.
- `server`: the MCTP stack, wrapping the external mctp-lib, with a dispatcher for IPC requests. On `main` it has no `main.rs`, because the image wiring lives in `target/`.
- `client-ipc`: the client side, talking to the server over an IPC channel.
- `transport-i2c`: carries MCTP over the I2C bus.
- `echo`: an echo loop used by tests.
- `transport-loopback`: lets MCTP run in a test without a physical bus. Demo branches only (`ocp-emea-demo-spdm-loopback` has an earlier loopback).

#### I2C (`services/i2c`)

A service so that many apps can share the I2C bus.

- `api`: the wire protocol, and a transport trait.
- `client`: an I2C client that looks like the standard Rust embedded I2C interface.
- `client-ipc`: the client's IPC transport.
- `server`, `server-runtime`: the server loop and request dispatch, including loopback and slave-mode handling.
- Master mode is complete. For slave (target) mode, receive works but event reporting is rough: the README says two event fields hold hard-coded values, and a HAL function it needs is missing.
- `backend-aspeed` (the ASPEED backend), `docs/` and `WIRE_REVIEW.md` exist only on `ocp-emea-demo-mem-bus` and `mctp-echo-pigweed-wmarone`.

#### Flash and crypto services

| Service | Description | Branches |
|---|---|---|
| `services/flash` | Lets other apps read, erase and write flash over IPC. | Demo branches have one version, backed by the ast10x0 flash controller. `earlgrey-hwe` has a separate version backed by its own drivers. |
| `services/crypto` (`api`, `client`) | A message format and client for asking the crypto service to verify a flash region (signature check). There is no server crate. | `ocp-global-demo-wip` only |
| `services/crypto` (full) | A software crypto service: SHA-256/384/512, HMAC, AES-256-GCM, and ECDSA P-256/P-384 behind a feature flag. One server file says ECDSA is not yet moved to the backend traits. | `ocp-emea-demo` branches only |

#### Test support (`services/test`)

`mock-downstream-device` is a mock BMC that boots, or fails to boot, on demand. It is on the demo branches only.

#### Empty shells

`services/storage` and `services/telemetry` contain only a doc comment and `#![no_std]`. They are identical on every branch I checked.

### 4.3 Hardware interfaces, platform and utilities

#### HAL (`hal/`)

- `hal/blocking`: the main interface crate. It has one module per area: digest (hashing), mac, cipher, ecdsa, key vault, GPIO ports, I2C hardware and device, and system control. These are traits with documentation, not hardware code. It also holds the `Flash` and `FlashDriver` traits.
- `hal/nb`: non-blocking I2C traits, including interrupt-driven slave mode.
- `hal/async`: a re-export of the standard async embedded interface, with nothing openPRoT-specific.
- On the demo branches, `hal/src` is a new crate for hardware-neutral vocabulary (field muxing, GPIO, I2C command words, resource tokens). It needs the nightly Rust compiler.
- On `earlgrey-hwe`, `hal/blocking/usb` adds USB descriptor and device traits.


#### Platform (`platform/`)

- `traits/hubris`: concrete-type crypto traits for the Hubris operating system's code generator.
- `impls/rustcrypto`: a working software implementation of AES-256-CTR and AES-256-GCM, and a controller.
- `impls/baremetal/mock`: test doubles for hashing, I2C and system control.
- `impls/hubris`, `impls/tock` and `impls/linux` are empty shells.

#### Utilities (`util/`)

On `main`:

- `error`: 32-bit error codes made from a module name and a code.
- `io`: the `RandomRead` trait and an I/O error module.
- `ipc`: wrappers for the kernel's IPC channels (initiator and handler traits, and a safe asynchronous transaction wrapper).
- `regcpy`: functions that copy byte slices to and from hardware registers.
- `types`: small shared types.

Added on other branches:

- Demo branches:
  - `sfdp`: the flash-size table parser.
  - `region`: tokens for owning memory regions, generated from the system config.
  - `service`: transport and dispatch traits, plus an in-process loopback.
  - `io`: more modules (byte source, byte window, storage).
- `earlgrey-hwe`:
  - `zfmt`: compact structured logging. Apps send binary events over IPC, and a log server renders text.
  - `panic`: a hook so the build can prove a binary cannot panic.
  - `ringbuffer`, `misc` (hexdump helpers): small helpers.

#### Drivers (`drivers/`)

- `usart`: a layered userspace serial driver (API, client, server). On `main` it is the only driver here.
- `flash/spi_flash.rs` (`earlgrey-hwe` only): a general SPI-NOR flash driver that reads the chip's size table, about 2,000 lines with unit tests. Quad-SPI mode is disabled in it.

### 4.4 Targets

#### ASPEED AST10x0 (`target/ast10x0`)

The main development platform. The `peripherals` crate has one module per hardware block:

| Module | What it drives | Completeness |
|---|---|---|
| `i2c` | Master and slave I2C, DMA, bus recovery | Largely implemented. Two TODOs in the slave status handling. |
| `i3c` | I3C controller | Substantial, but only an init and an interrupt test exist. |
| `smc` | The flash controllers (FMC and SPI): SPI-NOR access, memory-mapped reads, DMA | Mostly implemented, with a few TODOs, including no DMA read for large buffers. |
| `spimonitor` | The SPI monitor: per-command and per-address allow/block rules | Implemented |
| `scu` | System control: pin control, clocks, resets | Implemented |
| `gpio`, `sgpiom` | GPIO and serial GPIO | Implemented |
| `hace` | Hardware crypto engine (SHA, HMAC, AES) | Implemented. The QEMU emulator does not really perform AES. |
| `otp` | One-time-programmable memory and strap status | Implemented |
| `uart` | Serial port | Implemented |

Other parts of the target:

- `backend`: connects the I2C and USART services to the drivers.
- `board`: board start-up. Its SPI-monitor control is partial: resets are not polled or timed out, only one slot is used, and the violation count is hard-coded to 0.
- `pfr`: only an in-memory model of a software mailbox, not platform firmware resilience itself.
- `harness`: runners for QEMU and for the Raspberry Pi test setup.
- `tests`: kernel, IPC, peripheral and protocol tests (MCTP echo, SPDM responder and authentication).

What the other branches add:

- Demo branches:
  - `tests/integration`: 11 QEMU scenarios. Three are working scenarios (`mock_downstream_device`, `pldm_update`, `full_update`). Seven are failure cases that pass when the failure is detected (`device_hangs`, `corrupt_image`, `refused_update`, `transfer_error`, `offer_before_supervising`, `device_stays_down`). One is the withdrawal scenario `cancel_mid_transfer`.
  - `backend/flash`: adapts the flash controller to the flash service.
  - `boot_evidence`: turns boot-checkpoint signals into SGPIO pins.
  - Board files for a manifest and the mock BMC's reset and ready lines.
  - GPIO is restructured on this branch. Its `registers.rs` and `types.rs` are deleted, and `gpio/map.rs` and the `scu` pin-control files (`pinmux.rs`, `pins.rs`) are added. I did not check whether other branches rely on the old layout.
- `ocp-global-demo`: shared-flash and boot-from-flash tests, the reset-passthrough GPIO between the two boards, and scripts to deploy to the Pi.
- `i2c-mctp-throughput`: the throughput test.
- `spdm-measurements`: an SPDM measurements stress test.
- `smc-typestate`: the setup-order enforcement in the flash controller driver.
- `fix/ast10x0-spim`: extra files for the SPI monitor's address-privilege and command tables.
- `fix/ast10x0-i2c`: a single fix in the I2C slave code.

The tests README notes some failures from May: a kernel interrupt test times out on the physical board, an IPC test hangs under QEMU, and some tests are skipped on hardware. It also says wired Pi mode is not implemented. Several hardware constants are marked as unverified (system clock rate, MPU region count, SRAM size).

#### OpenTitan Earl Grey (`target/earlgrey`)

- **On `main`:** the starting point imported from Google. It has kernel bring-up (boot entry, memory protection, clocks), GPIO and pinmux drivers, generated register definitions, test signing keys, and runners for CW310, CW340, Verilator and QEMU. Its tests are small (GPIO, IPC, threads, UART). The README's build paths are out of date.
- **On `earlgrey-hwe`:** a much larger target.
  - Drivers: on-chip flash, SPI host, USB device controller, and UART.
  - USB protocol (`protocol/usb`): a device-side stack, USB serial (CDC-ACM) and USB firmware update (DFU 1.1).
  - Two firmware images:
    - `firmware/hwe`: five apps (system manager, log manager, USB manager, platform and flash server).
    - `firmware/transport`: a copy of that meant to be the manufacturing-time payload. It does firmware update and ownership transfer over SPI EEPROM or USB DFU, with host-side tests.
  - A platform service (strap pins, reset sequencing, muxes) and a system manager service (boot info, boot log, strap values).
  - Test runners that replace main's hard-coded one, with most newer tests running only on CW310, CW340 or real silicon. QEMU covers only the older tests and the SPI tests.

#### Caliptra / VeeR (`target/veer`)

A kernel target for the Caliptra RISC-V core, with IPC, threads, interrupt and syscall-latency tests, and a runner for the Caliptra emulator. The same on all branches. It is the least developed target, and I did not look further into it.

### 4.5 Tools

- `tools/i2c/i2c_monitor.py`: a monitor for I2C bus captures that can parse MCTP and SPDM. Its device-switching is a TODO.
- `tools/sgpiom`: generates SGPIO board config from JSON.
- `tools/flash_image`: builds a QEMU flash image from a slot layout, with tests. Demo branches only.

### 4.6 Not implemented on any branch

Searches covered `main`, `ocp-global-demo-wip`, `earlgrey-hwe` and `cq-demo-integration`. The other branches are older forks of `main` and were not searched, so an item could exist only there.

**Specified, but no code found:**

1. **Attestation evidence.** The spec requires a signed report of what firmware is running, in standard formats (RATS EAT or TCG Concise Evidence) delivered at SPDM measurement block 0xF0. No code matches. Separately, `docs/src/specification/services/attestation.md` is itself unfinished: its sections on claims, evidence formats, reference values, SPDM bindings, the local verifier and scenarios are all marked TODO.
2. **SPDM secure sessions.** `KEY_EXCHANGE`, `FINISH`, `PSK_*` and `KEY_UPDATE` (an encrypted channel) are not implemented. Neither are `SET_CERTIFICATE` and `GET_CSR`, so certificates cannot be provisioned over SPDM.
3. **SPDM requester operations.** The requester only builds a context. Challenge, measurement requests and certificate chain validation are listed as future work.
4. **Lockdown latch.** The orchestrator's "locked" state has no persistent design. `docs/src/design/orchestrator/orchestrator-platform.md` ends with a TODO on where the latch lives, what it gates and how it is cleared.
5. **PLDM Type 2** (sensors and platform monitoring). The spec requires types 0, 2 and 5. Types 0 and 5 are covered. I found no sensor handlers under `services/pldm`.
6. **PLDM pending-reset handshake.** `GAPS.md` says it "exists nowhere", not in the standard text, the PLDM library or the orchestrator.
7. **Persistent storage and telemetry.** Both services are empty, so nothing persists the anti-rollback floor or lockdown state.
8. **Firmware recovery, secure boot and policy management.** The services README lists these as TBD, and I found no implementation. `docs/src/specification/firmware_resiliency.md` has a "PRoT Resiliency: TBD" section.

**Partly implemented:**

- **Firmware update.** This works end to end in QEMU on the demo branches, but `GAPS.md` lists what a green run does not cover:
  - Automatic activation without an explicit ActivateFirmware command.
  - Authenticating the running image before its first release.
  - Backup-slot re-sync after a commit.
  - Boot progress over MCTP.
  - Retrying a data request, and a dropped response.
  - Some state-machine paths: the SVN update and commit-pending state, commit timeout, and recovery preempting an update.
  - The reset and ready lines are IPC channels in the tests, not real GPIOs.
  - The verifier is a stub that always passes, and refusals are recorded but not enforced.
  - The update gate says yes to everything.
- **Orchestrator actions on `main`.** Recover, authenticate, stage, activate, discard, sign attestation and lock down all fail safe. The demo branches add the update ones. I did not check recovery, attestation signing or lockdown there.
- **Crypto.** `main` has only the HAL traits and a software AES implementation, with nothing hooked up to SPDM. The demo branches add only a flash-region signature check client, with no server. The full software service exists only on the old EMEA demo branches. The AST10x0 hardware crypto engine driver exists but is not connected to a service.
- **SPDM crypto.** The hash and RNG shims use a stub client that always fails. The real client exists only on the demo branches.
- **MCTP.** There is no table mapping endpoint IDs to I2C addresses (`transport-i2c/src/sender.rs`), and the server does not yet read mctp-lib's configuration.
- **I3C and the SPI monitor.** Both have drivers, but I did not find services that use I3C. Write protection is, per a comment in the orchestrator config, expected to be guaranteed by board hardware.
- **Earl Grey.** It has no crypto or key-manager driver. The transport firmware's platform task is a placeholder (`firmware/transport/platform.rs`). The system manager hard-codes several values (firmware domain and straps). Binary logging output is not supported yet. Several READMEs are stale (the transport README still lists drivers as missing that now exist).
- **Platform impls.** Hubris, Tock and Linux are empty shells.
- **Documentation drift.** Examples: `services/orchestrator/sm/README.md` links to design files that do not exist on `main`, and the AST10x0 `smc` README names files that are not in the tree.



## 5. GitHub milestones versus actual progress

The project tracks work in five [GitHub milestones](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/milestones), all currently open. A milestone's percent-complete on GitHub only counts issues that have been formally closed, which can understate real progress: the Earl Grey driver work below, for example, mostly lives on the unmerged `earlgrey-hwe` branch, so GitHub shows little movement even where the code itself is substantial.

For each open issue, this section checked whether anything addressing it already exists in the code or docs, on any of the 28 branches, not just `main`. As with section 4, this was done by reading file trees and file contents, not by building or running anything, so "Done" below means "a real implementation/doc exists", not "tested and verified working".

### 5.1 Specification v0.5

All 10 issues in this milestone are open; none are closed.

Nearly everything here already has a home in `docs/src/specification/`; the issues mostly track splitting and finishing that content rather than starting from nothing.

| Issue | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| [#51](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/51) Attestation | Done | `docs/src/specification/services/attestation.md` is 680 lines, covering scope, the SPDM requester/responder roles, a local verifier, and evidence formats. The most complete doc of the ten. |
| [#46](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/46) High level architecture and block diagram | Done | `docs/src/specification/README.md` has a real block diagram (`openprot_diagram.svg`) and describes five architectural layers. A second, more repo-oriented doc, `docs/src/architecture.md`, covers the directory/build-system view. |
| [#45](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/45) Industry standards and specifications section | Done | Same README lists specific DMTF, TCG and NIST document numbers (e.g. SPDM's DSP0274), backed by three detailed protocol docs: `docs/src/specification/middleware/{spdm,mctp,pldm}.md`. |
| [#44](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/44) Goals | Done | A concrete bulleted list in `docs/src/specification/README.md` (write an OCP spec, build an open-source reference implementation, standardise hardware interfaces, etc.). |
| [#43](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/43) Background Section | Done | A real paragraph in the same README explaining the motivation (avoiding vendor lock-in and supply-chain risk). |
| [#50](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/50) Finalize high level markdown doc | Mostly done | That same README already combines the intro, background, goals, standards and architecture into one document, but is still tagged "v0.5 - Work in Progress". |
| [#42](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/42) Threat Model Definition | Partial | `docs/src/specification/threat_model.md` defines the assets and attacker profile (using the JIL smartcard attack-potential framework), but explicitly leaves the actual threat/mitigation table as a template for integrators to fill in. Some demo branches add an informal `docs/src/design/trust-boundaries.md` that defers to this file for the real analysis. |
| [#47](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/47) Firmware Resiliency section | Partial / mostly stub | `docs/src/specification/firmware_resiliency.md` has three paragraphs of background on NIST SP 800-193, but its two actual content sections, "PRoT Resiliency" and "Connected Device Resiliency", each just say "TBD". |
| [#49](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/49) Secure Boot | Not started | `docs/src/specification/services/README.md` lists "Secure Boot (TBD)" with no linked page, and secure boot gets one passing mention in the architecture section. No dedicated doc exists on any branch. |
| [#48](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/48) Firmware Recovery | Not started | Same services README lists "Firmware Recovery (TBD)"; no `firmware_recovery.md`-type file exists on any of the 28 branches. |

### 5.2 Infrastructure v0.1

8 issues are open, 4 are closed.

The four closed issues (remove the release workflow, remove the nightly Rust toolchain from CI, convert the build to Bazel, establish coding style standards) all match the repo's current state: it builds with Bazel only, and there's no release workflow.

| Issue | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| [#98](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/98) Document high-level repository structure | Done | `docs/src/architecture.md` already covers this: the `hal/`/`platform/traits`/`platform/impls` split, `drivers/`, `services/`, per-target directories, and how a reference firmware image is assembled. |
| [#96](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/96) Create a continuous integration system | Mostly done | `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs on every pull request: formatting and license checks, a C/C++ header check, Clippy (Rust's linter), a test job, a build job, and a separate security-audit job (dependency and static-analysis scanning). A separate test configuration already excludes hardware/simulator-tagged tests from the normal run, i.e. general and hardware-dependent tests are already split, which is what the issue asks for. |
| [#222](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/222) Bazel test execution scaffolding | Partial | Separate tagged test groups already exist for the Earl Grey Verilator simulator and the Caliptra emulator, plus a build-only (not run) target for the Caliptra FPGA board, which needs physical hardware. CI runs on what looks like a dedicated runner. No evidence yet of the FPGA/silicon tests actually executing in CI, or of documented workstation setup for hardware test rigs. |
| [#115](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/115) Execute heavyweight tests in the nightly workflow | Partial | A nightly workflow exists and runs on a schedule, excluding only hardware and explicitly-disabled tests — so it's broader than the normal PR run. It's unclear whether it specifically invokes the heavyweight Earl Grey Verilator suite mentioned in the issue, or just runs everything else by tag. |
| [#94](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/94) Establish review and committing procedures | Partial | `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `docs/src/development-process.md` already define a process: small vs. large changes, an RFC step needing Technical Steering Committee approval for large ones, and a fork-and-PR flow where CI must pass. There's no `CODEOWNERS` file, and no documented way to override a failing CI check. |
| [#97](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/97) Create codebase automation | Partial | The old `xtask` automation this issue asks to evaluate has already been removed (no trace of it on any branch). Automation now runs through Pigweed's `pw` launcher and a Bazel-based test/lint/presubmit configuration. No Bazel rules for test-coverage or binary-size reports were found, so that half of the issue looks untouched. |
| [#95](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/95) Establish a release process | Not started | No release workflow exists (removed per the closed #114), no documented tagging convention, and no mention of handling signed binaries. The one git tag present doesn't follow the naming scheme the issue proposes. |
| [#120](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/120) Integrate rust_doc builds with mdbook builds | Not started | The docs site is an mdbook book (`docs/book.toml`) deployed via its own workflow, but there's no sign anywhere of Rust's generated API documentation (rustdoc) being built or linked into it. |

### 5.3 M1.0 target/earlgrey - HW Integration Ready

12 issues are open, 1 is closed.

The milestone's goal is "an initial Earl Grey target able to support USB firmware update, GPIO configuration, reset sequencing and console test commands." The closed issue is Kernel bring-up. All the open-issue progress below sits entirely on the unmerged `earlgrey-hwe` branch, not in `main`.

| Issue | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| [#179](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/179) drivers/usb | Done | `target/earlgrey/drivers/usb_driver.rs` is a substantial USB device-controller driver, underpinning both a USB serial connection and the firmware-update protocol below. Has extensive test coverage. |
| [#180](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/180) drivers/eflash | Done | `target/earlgrey/drivers/eflash_driver.rs` wraps the chip's own flash controller with a read/write/erase permissions model, used by both firmware images and tested. |
| [#181](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/181) drivers/gpio | Done | Builds on the GPIO driver already on `main`, adding interrupt support used by the reset-sequencing logic below. Has its own test. |
| [#182](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/182) drivers/retram | Done | `target/earlgrey/util/ret_ram.rs` maps out "retention RAM" (a small amount of memory that survives a chip reset) to hold the boot log and reset reason, and is actively used to persist that state across resets. |
| [#187](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/187) Implement and integrate precise errors | Done | A shared error-code crate (a module name plus a code, packed into 32 bits) is used pervasively across the GPIO, SPI and flash driver. |
| [#188](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/188) DFU device update | Done | A generic USB firmware-update (DFU) protocol implementation, plus Earl Grey-specific logic that flashes images and hands over the chip's signing-key ownership to a new owner. Also has host-side test tooling. |
| [#189](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/189) Supervisor task | Done | A "system manager" service serves boot information over IPC and handles reboot requests by writing the hardware reset controller directly (addresses "boot services and RoT resets"). |
| [#190](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/190) Platform integration task | Done | A platform service reads the hardware configuration pins ("straps") sampled at boot, drives the chip's SPI/USB routing switches, and runs a full reset-sequencing state machine. Documented in its own README. |
| [#221](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/221) drivers/spi_host | Done | `target/earlgrey/drivers/spi_host.rs` is a working SPI driver using Rust's standard embedded-hardware interface, with its own tests. The same driver also covers milestone 5's duplicate #201 below. |
| [#186](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/186) UART console integration | Partial | A working serial console backend exists and is wired into logging, with a loopback test, but there's no interactive command shell — "console test commands" appears to mean automated test-harness commands rather than a user-facing shell, so this may be less complete than the milestone text implies. |
| [#183](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/183) drivers/sysctrl | Partial | Register definitions exist for the reset, clock and power managers, but only the reset manager is actually used by any code. The clock and power manager look like auto-generated skeletons with no driver logic written on top yet. |
| [#184](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/184) drivers/spidev | Not started | Only auto-generated register definitions and a software test mock exist; no real driver for the chip acting as an SPI peripheral (e.g. emulating an EEPROM) was found. |

### 5.5 M3.0 target/earlgrey - First Instruction Integrity

All 14 issues in this milestone are open; none are closed.

This milestone is about trusting the very first instruction Earl Grey's protected firmware runs: verifying it, updating it safely, and keeping track of its state across reboots. Like milestone 3, all the progress found here is on `earlgrey-hwe`, unmerged.

| Issue | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| [#205](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/205) Identify persistent configuration items | Done | The three hardware configuration pins ("soft straps") and their known combinations are defined and covered by a dedicated test. |
| [#206](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/206) Identify persistent runtime storage items | Done | The update manager writes firmware to flash using two alternating storage areas ("A/B slots"), and a boot-info test confirms the boot log, strap state and minimum accepted firmware version can all be read back. |
| [#212](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/212) Platform integration | Done | The same platform service credited under milestone 3's #190. |
| [#213](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/213) Implement event / error logging | Done | A purpose-built structured logging library sends binary, timestamped log events over IPC to a log server for rendering — matches the "machine readable" goal directly. |
| [#214](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/214) E2E Integration tests | Done | Real host-plus-target test pairs exist for USB firmware update, the configuration pins, boot info, logging, and the update manager — not just stubs. |
| [#201](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/201) drivers/spi_host | Done | Duplicate of milestone 3's #221 — same driver. |
| [#210](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/210) Implement payload policy, keys, domains, anti-rollback | Partial | The firmware manifest format (which carries the security version and signature) is parsed, the minimum accepted security version is tracked per boot stage, and separate production/development signing keys exist — but no distinct policy engine for production vs. development vs. test "domains" was found beyond the key sets themselves. |
| [#211](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/211) Payload updates via command protocol | Partial | The update mechanics (flashing A/B partitions, writing ownership data) work, but they're driven directly by the USB firmware-update protocol and raw SPI scanning rather than a separate higher-level command protocol layered on top. |
| [#204](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/204) Design and implement payload verification | Partial | The manifest format carries signature data and the build-time signing-key infrastructure exists, but no code that actually checks a signature at boot time was found — this likely relies on OpenTitan's existing chip boot ROM rather than reimplementing verification here. |
| [#209](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/209) Crypto services | Partial | Shared hardware-abstraction traits for hashing and MAC (message authentication code) operations exist, but they're generic groundwork identical to what's already on `main`, not something built specifically for this milestone. |
| [#207](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/207) Investigate FW update protocols | Partial | No written comparison document exists, but Earl Grey has in practice settled on USB firmware update plus SPI flash scanning. A separate, older spec doc argues for a different protocol (PLDM) and appears to predate or ignore that decision. |
| [#203](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/203) Design command transport protocol | Partial | USB firmware update is implemented, and the message-transport protocol used elsewhere in the project (MCTP) exists as shared infrastructure, but no "SPI mailbox" protocol was found — the SPI path in use is flash scanning, not a mailbox-style register protocol. |
| [#202](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/202) drivers/spi_eeprom | Not started | The branch's own README lists this driver as an explicit, unchecked TODO. |
| [#208](https://github.com/OpenPRoT/openprot/issues/208) Integrate internal file system | Not started | Only a design doc mentioning Pigweed (the framework the kernel is built on) in general terms exists; no key-value store code was found. |



## 6. Summary

openPRoT is building a shared, open-source Rust firmware stack for a Platform Root of Trust: a small chip that verifies other devices' firmware and mediates their updates. `main` already has a working core: I2C, MCTP, SPDM and PLDM services, and an orchestrator that sequences boot and updates for the ASPEED AST10x0 target.

The most complete view of that update story, end to end in QEMU, lives on an unmerged stack of demo branches (`ocp-global-demo-wip` and what it contains), built mainly by Christina Quast, JesseMelon and Anthony Rocha. The single largest body of unmerged work, however, is `earlgrey-hwe`: a substantial, largely separate port to OpenTitan's Earl Grey chip (USB, flash, GPIO, update and ownership-transfer logic, logging), led by Chris Frantz, that `main` has drifted 261+ commits away from.

That gap between branches and `main` also explains most of the mismatch between GitHub's milestones and what the repo actually contains: of the 54 open milestone issues, nearly half (23) already have real work behind them, and 15 of those sit entirely on `earlgrey-hwe`. However, gaps still remain in a few specific places: TPM 2.0 support (milestone 4) hasn't been started anywhere, and a handful of specification pages (secure boot, firmware recovery) and security-critical behaviours (real signature verification, a release process, persistent storage for anti-rollback/lockdown state) are still missing or stubbed out across every branch.



## Glossary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| RoT / eRoT | Root of Trust: the security chip running openPRoT. "eRoT" is the same thing, short for external RoT. |
| Protected device / mock BMC | The device the RoT guards. A BMC (baseboard management controller) is the management chip on a server board. The demo uses a stand-in "mock BMC" (later renamed "mock downstream device"). |
| OCP | Open Compute Project. The EMEA and global demos were built for its events. |
| Orchestrator | The state machine that decides when devices boot, when an update may proceed, and what to do on failure (see section 1). |
| IPC | Inter-process communication: how separate apps on the kernel call each other. |
| Flash | The non-volatile memory chips that hold firmware. |
| A/B slots | Devices keep two copies of their firmware. A new image is written to the spare slot, tried, and the old one remains as a fallback. |
| SVN / anti-rollback floor | Security version number. The floor is the lowest firmware version the RoT will accept, so a known-vulnerable older image cannot be installed. |
| QEMU | An emulator, used to run firmware tests without hardware. |
| EVB | Evaluation board, a development board for a chip. |
| CI | Continuous integration: automated builds and tests that run on every pull request. |
| TPM | Trusted Platform Module: an industry-standard security chip interface, separate from openPRoT's own RoT design. |
| PCR | Platform Configuration Register: a TPM register that records a running tally ("measurement") of what firmware has booted, used for attestation. |
| DICE | Device Identifier Composition Engine: a method of deriving device identity keys layer by layer through the boot process. |
| Soft straps | Hardware configuration pins sampled once at boot to decide how the chip should behave (e.g. which mode to start in). |
| Retention RAM | A small area of memory that keeps its contents across a chip reset, used to carry boot state from one boot to the next. |
